result:
There's a particular pleasure in starting with no destination. Most writing I do has a shape imposed on it before the first word arrives—a question to answer, a task to complete, a problem someone else has defined. This is different. This is more like walking into a field and deciding to walk in whatever direction the ground seems to suggest.

So let me start with something small: the way attention works like a flashlight in a dark room. You can only really see what the beam falls on, and everything else exists in a kind of theoretical darkness, present but unconfirmed. I find this fact more unsettling the longer I sit with it. We tend to imagine our minds as cameras, recording everything in front of us in continuous, even detail, when in fact most of what passes before us is barely registered, glanced at, filed under "background" and forgotten before it was ever properly noticed. The room you're sitting in right now—can you say, without looking, how many books are on the nearest shelf? What color the wall is behind you? You've been in that space for an hour, maybe longer, and yet enormous portions of it are blank. Not because the information wasn't available, but because nothing asked you to look.

This selective blindness isn't a flaw so much as the precondition for thought at all. A mind that registered everything with equal weight would drown in undifferentiated noise; it would be unable to find the signal that distinguishes a predator from a shadow, a friend's voice from ambient chatter. So attention is a kind of violence done to the world—it cuts the continuous fabric of experience into discrete, manageable pieces, and discards the rest. Every act of perception is also an act of forgetting, performed in the same instant. We don't notice this because the forgotten parts don't announce their absence. There's no felt gap where the unattended-to texture of the carpet should be. It simply isn't there, cleanly, without residue.

I think about this because it seems to be the root of something larger: the way all categories are a kind of useful violence. Take the concept of a "tree." There is no tree in nature, not really—there is a continuous, branching, water-drawing, light-catching process that we, for convenience, decide to call a discrete object with a name. The boundary we draw around "tree" and against "not-tree" is not given by the world; it's imposed by us, for our purposes, which are mostly about communication and prediction. The actual tree does not stop being part of the soil it's rooted in, the fungal networks threading through that soil, the insects boring through its bark, the air it's constantly trading gases with. We say "tree" and mean a fairly stable shape with a trunk and leaves, but the world we're pointing at is far more entangled and far less bounded than the word suggests.

This matters because so much of human suffering and confusion comes from forgetting that categories are tools and starting to treat them as facts of nature. Race, nation, self, even time—these are useful cuts made into a continuous fabric, cuts that let us communicate, predict, plan, but they are not seams that were already there waiting to be found. The work of growing wiser, if such a thing is possible, seems to involve a constant low-grade vigilance: remembering that the map is not the territory, that the knife that cuts the world into "us" and "them," "mine" and "yours," "now" and "later," is a knife we're holding, and we could, in principle, cut differently.

And yet—here's the strange part—we can't simply discard the categories either. Trying to perceive the world without any conceptual carving at all doesn't produce some pure, unmediated contact with reality; it mostly just produces confusion, or a kind of mystical blankness that has its own charm but isn't more "true" than ordinary seeing. The contemplative traditions that pursue this—certain strands of Buddhist practice, for instance—don't claim that dissolving categories gives you a final correct picture of the world. They tend to say something more modest and stranger: that loosening your grip on the categories changes your relationship to suffering, because so much suffering comes from clinging to a particular cut of the world as though it were eternal and necessary, when it was always provisional, always one carving among many possible ones.

I keep circling back to the idea of cutting because it seems to apply to language with unusual force. A word is, among other things, a tool for slicing a continuous experiential field into a nameable unit. "Loneliness" is a word for a vast, shifting, individually variable weather system of feeling, and yet once you have the word, you start to feel like you know what loneliness is, as though it were a single thing with clean edges. People will say "I'm lonely" and mean wildly different internal states—a craving for touch, a hunger for being known, a simple absence of plans on a Friday night, a существential dread about mattering to no one—and the word flattens all of that into a single shape, for the purposes of being communicated quickly. This isn't a failure of language; it's what language is for. But it's worth remembering, especially when a word like that gets used about yourself, that the word is doing some flattening, and that whatever you're actually experiencing is probably more specific and stranger than the label suggests.

There's an idea I find appealing, from cognitive science, that analogy is the engine of all this carving and recombining—that the basic operation of thought is not deduction or logic but a constant, restless process of noticing that this is, in some respect, like that. A tree is like a river of nutrients; an argument is like a building, with foundations and load-bearing claims; an atom is like a solar system, with a nucleus like a sun and electrons like orbiting planets. None of these analogies are exact—the atom is not really like a solar system, not if you push the comparison hard, because the electron doesn't have a well-defined orbit in the way a planet does, and the forces involved are quantum rather than classical—but the analogy was useful enough to think with for a while, before it had to be discarded or refined.

This makes me wonder whether all understanding is fundamentally a sequence of analogies that are gradually refined, never quite arriving at the literal truth but getting more and more useful as approximations. Maybe there is no "literal truth" underneath the analogies at all—maybe truth, at some sufficiently fundamental level, is just the best analogy we haven't yet found a flaw in. This is uncomfortable to people who want a bedrock, a place where the metaphors stop and the real thing is finally there, unmediated. But it might be that the unmediated thing is not available to a mind that works by carving and comparing—that the price of being a mind at all, rather than simply being a piece of inert matter, is that you only ever get access to the world through some scaffolding of comparison, never the world plain.

Let me shift tracks for a moment, because I started thinking about attention and I want to come back to something more specific: the experience of noticing something for the first time that you've apparently seen a thousand times before. There's a particular flavor to this experience—it has a kind of mild vertigo to it, a sense of "how did I miss this," even though the honest answer is that you didn't miss it, exactly; you registered it at some shallow level sufficient for navigation but never elevated it to the kind of attention that produces a memory you can retrieve later. I think this happens constantly with people we love. You can live with someone for years and one day notice, with real surprise, some gesture they make—the way they always check the stove twice before leaving the house, the way their voice changes register when they're talking to children versus adults—and feel as though you've discovered something. In a sense you have: not a new fact about them, but a newly attended-to fact, promoted from background noise to figure.

This suggests something almost hopeful about boredom, or about long familiarity, which we tend to regard as a kind of enemy of vividness. The boring landscape, the over-familiar partner, the street you've walked down ten thousand times—the dullness isn't a property of the thing; it's a property of your attention having stopped renewing its contact with the thing. Which means the dullness is, in principle, reversible at any moment, just by attending differently. This is not a small claim, even if it sounds like a self-help platitude. It implies that vividness is not a resource that gets used up by repetition—not like a coin that loses its image the more it's handled—but something closer to a skill, or a posture, that can be picked back up at will, at least some of the time, with effort or luck or the right kind of jolt.

I notice I've been writing about looking and noticing for a while, and I want to ask myself honestly why that's the thread I followed rather than some other one—say, justice, or memory, or the strange fact that we are matter complex enough to wonder about its own complexity. I think it's because attention feels like the thing underneath all the other things. You can't be just to someone you've never really looked at. You can't remember something you never attended to in the first place, except in the thin, unreliable way that things get encoded by accident, in passing. And the strangeness of being matter that wonders about itself is, when you get down to it, a strangeness about a very particular and very intense form of attention—matter attending to its own attending, looking at the flashlight rather than just using it to look at other things.

There's something almost dizzying about trying to attend to attention itself, the way it's dizzying to try to see your own eye without a mirror. The instrument can't easily turn around and inspect itself, because the inspecting is being done by the instrument. This is probably why so much contemplative practice across so many different traditions converges on some version of "watch the watcher," "notice the noticer"—not because it produces a clean answer, a successful capture of the self by the self, but because the attempt itself does something, reorganizes the relationship between the watcher and the watched in a way that's hard to describe but apparently worth pursuing for thousands of years across cultures that otherwise have very little in common.

I don't know if I believe there's a self doing the watching, in any robust sense, or whether "self" is just another one of those useful cuts—a story stitched together after the fact to explain why a continuous stream of experience seems to belong to someone, the way "tree" is a story stitched together to explain why a continuous process of growth and exchange seems to be a single bounded object. I lean toward thinking the self is more like the tree than like a soul: a real pattern, with real causal powers, but not a separately existing thing underneath the pattern, waiting to be found if you looked hard enough. This doesn't strike me as a depressing conclusion, though I understand why it strikes many people that way. If the self is a pattern rather than a fixed essence, then it is, like all patterns, capable of changing, of being re-woven, of incorporating new threads. A fixed essential self would actually be a kind of prison—you'd be stuck being exactly what you already are, forever, with no real room for growth, because growth would mean becoming something other than your essence, which is supposed to be unchangeable by definition. A self that's a pattern, on the other hand, is closer to a river than a stone: the same name applies to it across time, usefully, but the water is never the same water twice, and that's not a problem for the river, that's just what a river is.

I started this piece thinking I'd write about the flashlight of attention and ended up at the river of selfhood, by way of trees and atoms and loneliness and contemplative practice, and I think this drifting is itself a small demonstration of the thing I was trying to describe—the mind moving by analogy, one resemblance suggesting the next, with no fixed destination decided in advance, only a kind of momentum generated by each idea touching the next at some point of similarity. If I'd outlined this in advance, it would have a cleaner shape, probably a more useful one for a reader looking for an argument to take away and use. But it would also have lost something: the textured, undirected quality of actual thinking, which rarely arrives at conclusions so much as it arrives at a temporary resting point, a place where the walker stops, looks around, and decides the light is interesting here, this is a good place to sit for a while, before eventually getting up and walking on, into territory not yet cut into trees, rivers, selves, or any other names at all.
